What's the difference between Linux and BSD?

BSD is Unix, and all the good and bad that comes with. It's ostensibly the kernel before Linus decided to go off and do his own thing, but in reality it has evolved quite a bit in the interim, all while trying to remain true to the Unix ideals.

There's a WORLD of difference between the two. First off, you have to know the history of where they came from.

In the beginning was Unix. Unix was owned by AT&T (Bell labs), and used in many aspects of the computing world... including teaching. But, somewhere along the way (late 1980's), Unix updated (to v6 or v7, I can't remember which) and changed their ToC to say that Unix couldn't be used in a formal instructional environment anymore. They also amped up the price, and did some other things AT&T is know to do.

So, this "angered" three people/groups. The University of California - Berkeley, a student named Linus Torvalds, and a professor named Andrew Tanenbaum.

First, Professor Tanenbaum was teaching Unix to his CS students, but could no longer do so, after the update... so he created a monolithic kernel called Minix. This was a "clone" of Unix, and it allowed him to continue teaching POSIX in his classroom without having to jump through a TON of legal loopholes.

Secondly, Linus was a poor student who couldn't afford Unix, so he created Linux... a FREE microkernel that anyone could use.

But, the problem with both of these is that they were created from the ground-up, to avoid legal repercussions with Unix and Bell Labs. So, needless to say, there were some major differences, and changes.

The UCB didn't like this, because they needed to teach Unix in their classrooms, so they came up with a third option: create BSD. Initially, BSD had a handful of Unix code, but not enough to hinder its instruction... UCB just had to pay roayalties to Bell. But, after some time, UCB decided that enough was enough, they rewrote these parts of the code, and made a complete divorce from Unix.

Now, given everyone's different paths and choices, each kernel ended up being different from each other. If you're used to a Linux machine, you'll notice that you have two etc directories in /etc/ as well as in /usr/etc/. This is an old holdover from Unix, and Linux primarily uses the root version, /etc/, where BSD primarily uses the usr version, /usr/etc/.

Also, Linux tends to be just a kernel (unless you're talking about GNU), and BSD is a fully-fledged OS.

The differences more noticeable in the licensing of the two, as that's what REALLY sets them apart:

Linux uses GPLv2, and BSD uses... well... BSD licensing. And this is important to the userbase, and the ecosystem...

For starters, they're not compatible with one another, and they are also compatible/incompatible with other licensing schemes. This is why zfs will never be packaged with Linux, because its licensing doesn't work with GPL... but it's packaged with BSD. The list can go on and on, but that's pretty much the gist of things here.

After that, you have to understand how software and drivers work:

Under GPLv2, if you use code to make new code, it HAS to be open for everyone's benefit. In other words, if you make a driver for your graphics card, on Linux, you MUST send that code to Linus for consideration on if it will be freely implemented into the Linux kernel. You can NOT close the source to your driver, and you can NOT withhold that data.

Under BSD, things are very different. If you do the same with BSD, you can add your driver to your system, close the source for the whole thing, and start charging people for using your OS. This is beneficial to companies, like Apple, who used Darwin (a form of BSD) and installed the closed-source iTunes, and now FORBIDS users from using "illegal-free" copies of its OS... they've closed the source to Darwin, re-branded it as OSX, and are now charging customers for it (through hardware).
